title: Schrödinger Eigenfunction Method for Long-Horizon Stochastic Optimal Control
one_liner: By learning the eigenfunctions of a quantum-like operator, you can plan optimal actions far into the future without the memory and time blowup that plagues normal long-horizon control methods.
lead: Planning optimal actions over many time steps — like steering a robot arm toward a distant target — normally requires computer memory and time that grows with the length of the plan. This paper shows that when the forces acting on the system have a special structure (they point downhill from a peak, the way gravity pulls toward a valley), you can recast the planning problem as finding the natural vibration patterns of an operator from quantum mechanics. Learning those patterns with a neural network, using a corrected training objective, gives you control that stays accurate even for plans hundreds of steps into the future.

problem.h2: Long-horizon control explodes in memory and time
paras: In random optimal control, you choose actions over time to minimize cost (or maximize reward) while the world has randomness in it. For instance, a robot planning 100 steps into the future needs to answer: if I do action now, will the state move closer to my goal after 100 steps? To compute this, normal methods simulate forward 100 times or build a tree of outcomes, both of which take memory and computation that grow with the horizon (the number of steps). At horizon 500, you are moving colossal amounts of data.

A beginner might try to just run the standard control algorithm — like dynamic programming or value iteration — but the algorithm slows down by a factor equal to the horizon each time you lengthen the plan. Worse, the quality of the answer deteriorates exponentially: errors in early decisions compound over time, and random fluctuations grow louder the further out you plan.

callout.html: Long-horizon random optimal control requires memory and time that scale with horizon T, and planning accuracy decays exponentially as T grows.

panels.title: 1. Normal long-horizon planning
panels.caption: Simulate forward, track every branch, memory explodes with horizon T.

panels.title: 2. The structure: forces point downhill
panels.viz_args: Gradient drift: uncontrolled system rolls down a valley.
panels.caption: When forces follow a potential (like gravity in a bowl), math simplifies.

panels.title: 3. Recast as a Schrödinger operator
panels.caption: Eigenvalues become the long-horizon control signal; higher ones decay to noise.

panels.title: 4. Fix the loss function
panels.viz_args: Relative loss = (L phi / phi) - lambda. Removes hidden bias.
panels.caption: Old loss implicitly reweights eigenfunctions; new relative loss corrects it.

panels.title: 5. Control scales like space, not time
panels.caption: Memory and time now scale with state dimension d, not horizon T.

steps.text: Check if the uncontrolled system (forces with no action) points downhill from a potential.
Transform the Bellman equation (which tracks expected future cost) into a linear partial differential equation ruled by an operator L.
Under the gradient drift condition, L is unitarily equivalent to a Schrödinger operator (the quantum mechanical operator) with a discrete spectrum of eigenfunctions.
Train a neural network to approximate the dominant eigenfunctions using a corrected relative loss that avoids hidden reweighting bias.
Combine the learned eigenfunctions (which encode the long-horizon structure) with a short-horizon solver near the terminal time to get the full optimal control.

paras: The paper changes the loss function used when training a neural network to learn the eigenfunctions (natural vibrations of the Schrödinger operator). Existing loss functions — whether physics-informed or variational — accidentally reweight the optimization in a way that biases you away from learning the dominant eigenfunction cleanly. The paper proposes a new 'relative loss' that strips away that hidden reweighting.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: implicit reweighting bias
hidden.name: The unintended reweighting hidden in the loss
paras: When you train a neural network to find an eigenfunction (a special function where applying the operator just scales it by a single number), you need a loss function — a measure of how wrong are you — to guide training. A natural choice is to make the loss small when applying the operator gives a result close to scaling the function. But this loss happens to implicitly reweight each point in space by the value of the function squared, biasing the optimization toward learning a warped version of the function instead of the true one.

The paper measures and names this bias: it is the stationary distribution of the uncontrolled system (where probability accumulates under the random walk). Existing variational and physics-informed neural network (PINN) losses all suffer from this reweighting. The relative loss removes it by dividing the operator result by the function value before comparing to the scaling number, eliminating the squared-function weighting entirely.

heat.caption: Darker means more bias or error. True eigenfunction learning requires the relative loss.

reads.html: Old losses accidentally favor certain parts of the space over others because they weight each point by how probable it is under the uncontrolled system. The relative loss divides the error by the function value to undo this weighting, leaving you learning the true shape.

The stationary distribution of the uncontrolled drift induces a weighted norm in the loss function. The variational loss lives in this weighted norm, causing bias. The relative loss uses the operator result divided by the function value, compared against the scaling number, all in an unweighted norm.

mechanism.h2: Why this method works: connecting quantum operators to control
paras: The magic starts with a mathematical fact: when the uncontrolled system (no action taken) has forces that point downhill from a peak, the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation — which is normally a complex nonlinear partial differential equation that encodes optimal control — becomes a simpler linear equation. That equation is governed by an operator, and under the gradient drift assumption, the operator has a discrete spectrum (like the energy levels of a quantum harmonic oscillator).

The eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of this operator encode the long-horizon control structure: the dominant eigenfunction gives you the control action, and because it is an eigenfunction, applying the operator just scales it by a single number — the solution does not change shape over time, only its overall magnitude. This is why you can compute optimal control far into the future without simulating: the eigenfunction structure is stable. No need to recompute or resimulate at each step; the eigenfunction works for all time.

However, learning this eigenfunction from data is tricky. The existing losses accidentally measure error in a weighted norm that favors high-probability regions (where the uncontrolled system naturally goes). That bias pulls the learned eigenfunction toward the wrong shape. The relative loss switches the measuring rod: instead of measuring the error in the natural weighted norm, it measures the error after dividing the operator result by the function value, in an unbiased norm, removing the hidden reweighting. With the correct loss, the neural network converges to the true eigenfunction.

stages.s: Control trajectory (state at each time step, action taken, cost accrued)
Identify: is the uncontrolled drift a gradient (forces point downhill)?
Recast as operator equation: Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman becomes eigenvalue problem
Learn eigenfunction: train neural network with relative loss (unbiased)
Correct near end: add short-horizon optimization for terminal part
Long-horizon optimal control policy (memory and time scale as state dimension, not horizon)

math.words: The relative loss for learning an eigenfunction: sum over all sample points of (operator applied to learned eigenfunction, divided by the learned eigenfunction, minus the learned eigenvalue) squared, plus a regularization term.
math.equation: R_Rel(phi) = sum_i || (L phi_i / phi_i) - lambda ||^2 + alpha * R_reg(phi)
symbols: the operator (like a quantum Schrödinger operator for this system)
the learned eigenfunction (a neural network outputs this)
the eigenfunction evaluated at sample point i
the learned eigenvalue (a number, trainable parameter)
the operator applied and then scaled down by the eigenfunction value
the weight controlling how much regularization to apply
a regularization term (keeps the network from blowing up)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at point x=3: the true eigenfunction is phi(3)=2.0, eigenvalue is lambda=5.0.
The operator L phi(3) should equal 5.0 * 2.0 = 10.0 (by definition of eigenfunction).
With the relative loss: (L phi / phi) - lambda = (10.0 / 2.0) - 5.0 = 5.0 - 5.0 = 0. Error is 0.
If the network guesses phi(3)=1.9 instead: (L phi / phi) - lambda = (9.75 / 1.9) - 5.0 ≈ 5.13 - 5.0 = 0.13. Small error, guides correction.
Old loss would have measured ||L phi - lambda*phi||^2_weighted, which is biased by how often the system visits x=3. Relative loss treats all sample points fairly.

math.note: The relative loss eliminates the unintended weighting by dividing the operator result by the function value before comparing to the scaling number, making the learning problem unbiased.

charts.title: Old methods (PINNs, variational loss)
charts.note: Performance crashes as horizon lengthens. Biased eigenfunction learning and exponential error accumulation compound.

charts.title: This paper (relative loss)
charts.note: Unbiased eigenfunction learning keeps accuracy high. Control structure remains stable because it is built on true eigenfunctions.

items.html: If the uncontrolled forces do not point downhill from a potential (e.g., they swirl or have curl), the Schrödinger operator equivalence breaks down. The method does not apply to general nonlinear dynamics.

Learning an eigenfunction is harder than supervised learning. If the network is too small, the regularizer (a term that keeps the network weights from blowing up) too strong, or the relative loss still has numerical issues at the edges of the state space, convergence can stall.

The dominant eigenfunction encodes the infinite-horizon cost. If the goal is a finite-horizon terminal cost (cost only at step T, zero elsewhere), a correction near the end is needed; ignoring this leaves the final actions suboptimal.

Combine the learned dominant eigenfunction with a second neural network that optimizes the terminal part (the last few steps). This hybrid approach combines the strengths: infinite-horizon structure from eigenfunction, finite-horizon flexibility from short-horizon optimization.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple long-horizon random optimal control task: for instance, a particle moving in 2D space under random noise, where you control a force to steer toward a goal. Use a potential well as the uncontrolled drift (e.g., gravity pulling toward a target region). Implement the standard (biased) variational eigenfunction loss and the new relative loss on the same task. Train a neural network on each, learn the top eigenfunction, and generate control trajectories for horizons from 10 to 500 steps. Measure the average distance from goal at horizon 500 and the total computation time.
demo.metric_eq: Control error = distance to goal under learned policy / distance to goal under optimal policy (lower is better)
demo.closing: The relative loss should keep error constant or near-constant across all horizons, while the biased loss error should grow exponentially with horizon length.
